content.text: Steve-- I may be badly misunderstanding you, but if the indexes have to be able to reflect arbitrary uses of "resource, subject, action, environment attributes" and since XACML can use those attributes inside of some pretty byzantine calculations, is this really a strong restriction on the functionality? Isn't it so very close to a full XML database that we might as well use a component like eXist-db or something similar? In that case, do we need to think about supporting multiple indexing systems, ala Trippi and the RI?

Or are you saying that the mere appearance of a given attribute, regardless of its use, is the only thing that matters and so an index would contain almost entirely boolean fields labelled by attribute name?

Essentially it's the latter - the XML indexing for XML database back-ends is based on indexing the document's Target - on all of the subject, resource, action and environment attributes, regardless of their usage.  Rules are ignored by the indexing.
So it would be a case of replicating the same basic level of indexing.

In fact the overall indexing strategy for XML database back-ends could be improved/optimised; though the overall function of the policy index is to be able to get a candidate set of relevant policies for evaluation.  The PDP's evaluation of these then determines the actual relevancy - so if you like the policy index is a pre-filtering mechanism to limit the number of policies evaluated.  (In the non-FeSL XACML engine all policies in the directory are evaluated, plus any attached via a POLICY datastream to the object being requested.)

Right, I now understand why the full machinery of an XML database might arguably be more than enough. On the other hand, would the ability to use multiple possible backends for policy indexing still be interesting to users? In that case, it might be worth writing against something like XQJ while providing sample index configs for a few dbs and packaging one light db (eXist?).

It's now clear to me that building a database to support this functionality wouldn't be difficult. I guess I'm just playing devil's advocate and asking whether we instead can use an existing off-the-shelf part with its own community of support.

I'd support continuing being able to use Berkeley DB XML at least for the short term; at least until we have a better understanding of FeSL use in practice and its requirements on the indexing back-end.  It would be great to find a component that would provide the interfacing to different XML databases (I had a look around for these for the 3.5 release; but didn't find anything with the necessary coverage).
In case it is not clear, eXist is now supported (as of 3.5) as an alternative to using either the built-in file policy index or Berkeley DB XML.

I'd agree that using an off-the-shelf component would be a preferable route; however it may be that the indexing requirements are so light-weight that use of an XML database is overkill, and that building our own simple index could in fact be more performant.
Better guidance on these issues will, in my opinion, come from people's experiences with increased adoption of FeSL.
I would be surprised if a purpose-built component would
not
be more performant. {grin} I guess I'm worrying more about maintenance costs, portability of data, etc.
The interface is tricky. The closest thing I could find was writing against XQJ, supported by eXist, MarkLogic, Sedna, Oracle, BaseX, but
not
dbXML. (I'm a little concerned about dbXML's forward path-- it doesn't seem to have been released since 2009.) And XQJ would do nothing to help with configuring the various possible stores.

But I agree completely that the guidance should come from use. It may very well turn out that virtually no one uses anything but the default component, in which case time spent on portability would have been wasted, but time spent beefing up the default component would be the best investment.
I think I rejected the XML database APIs I came across as none supported both eXist and DB XML with sufficient coverage and were being actively maintained.

Interesting that the newest DB XML release is now over 2 years old... perhaps we should consider deprecating support for it.  Which then may remove some restrictions when selecting what to write against API-wise.

That's exactly what I was thinking. But I think you've already hit the nail on the head-- we'd have to see what the demand for portability/scalability really is to understand what the right way to go forward would be.
No further releases planned for 3.x

FeSL has a default policy index implementation of FilePolicyIndex (since 3.5) .  This is a basic memory-cached, file-backed policy index.  It always returns the full set of policies known to it (it does no filtering based on the request) - similar to the legacy XACML implementation.
As such it is suitable for a relatively small number of policies.

This index could be enhanced to provide indexing and better caching to provide a performant alternative to an XML database-backed policy index.  The full functionality of an XML database is not required to support FeSL - what is required is indexed access to policies based on (configurable) resource, subject, action, environment attributes.
An option could be to do the indexing in an SQL database.
